The spec is exceptionally thorough — no `[NEEDS CLARIFICATION]` markers, and the inherited 001 spec already settles username-format scope and concurrency-out-of-scope. My scan found a handful of decisions the spec made by assumption that would change acceptance tests if decided differently. I have 5 queued; I'll ask them one at a time.

---

**Question:** When a reset succeeds on an account that is currently locked out from five failed logins, should the reset also clear the lock and the failed-login count, or leave the account locked until `unlock` is run? (FR-038)

Why it matters: a forgotten password is the most common reason an account gets locked, so if a reset leaves the lock in place, the user still cannot log in after resetting and the administrator has to run a second command to finish the recovery.

**Recommended:** Option A — The user's description says `reset` "sets the new password" and nothing more, the existing `passwd` command already sets a password without unlocking, and `unlock` is the one command that owns lock state. Keeping that boundary means no existing security behaviour changes by surprise; the cost is one extra administrator command in the locked case, which is already an administrator-assisted flow.

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| A | Leave lock state and failed-login count untouched, exactly as `passwd` does. A locked account still reports `account locked` / 4 after a successful reset until `unlock` is run. (current spec) |
| B | A successful `reset` also clears the lock and resets the failed-login count to zero, so one reset fully restores access. |
| C | A successful `reset` resets the failed-login count to zero but does not clear an existing lock. |
| D | `reset` refuses to act on a locked account at all, requiring `unlock` first. |
| Short | Provide a different short answer (<=5 words) |

You can reply with the option letter (e.g., "A"), accept the recommendation by saying "yes" or "recommended", or provide your own short answer.
